transcript.text: induction hob keeps turnin off after 5-10 mins on high, have to keep restartin it. drives me nuts. any1 know y?

That pattern, fine at first and then cutting out after 5–10 minutes on high, usually means the hob is protecting itself rather than something being broken. 1. Overheating protection. Induction hobs have a cooling fan and temperature sensors on the electronics underneath. If hot air can't escape, the hob shuts down. That can happen with a cramped space or blocked vents below, a drawer packed right up underneath, or an oven running below. It can also happen if the fan has stopped working. High settings make the most heat, which fits your symptom.
2. A built-in time or boost limit. Many hobs only run boost (or P) for about 5–10 minutes, then drop back to a lower setting or switch off for safety. That's normal, not a fault.
3. The touch controls being triggered. A boil-over, steam condensing on the panel, or a pan handle or utensil resting on the controls can make the hob shut off as a safety measure. 1. Watch the display when it cuts out. If the zone just drops from boost to a lower number, that's the timer (normal). If it shows a code (often with an E or H) or a flashing symbol, that points to overheating or a fault.
2. Keep the control area dry and clear. Wipe it, and keep pans and utensils off it. If the cut-outs stop, it was the controls being triggered.
3. Check the airflow. With the hob off and cool, look at the space directly underneath (drawer or cupboard) and clear anything pressed up against the base or vents. If it only cuts out with the oven on or the space crowded, it's a ventilation issue.
4. Listen for the fan. On high you should hear a soft whirr from underneath, often carrying on for a while after you switch off. If it's silent even with the hob on high for a few minutes, the cooling fan may have failed. That's a job for an engineer, as it means taking the hob out. If none of that changes anything, the next suspects are a temperature sensor or the power board. Those need an engineer, and the make and model would help then.
its Samsung. started after a new drawer unit was fitted under it last month. fan goes loud then it cuts out, sometimes a code flashes but i cant read it. not pulling the drawer out tho

That detail about the new drawer unit is the big clue. Starting right after it was fitted, the fan roaring and then the hob cutting out with a code is the classic pattern of the hob overheating and shutting itself down to protect the electronics. The loud fan is a good sign: it suggests the fan is working but can't shift the hot air. Induction hobs need a clear air gap underneath, often around 20 mm, plus a path for air to get in and out (usually at the front or back of the cabinet). A drawer unit fitted too high, a drawer box sitting right up against the hob's base, or the rear gap being boarded off would all cause exactly this. You don't need to remove the drawer to test this: 1. Simply open the drawer, then with the hob off and cool, shine a torch in. Look at whether the drawer box or anything in it (pans, lids, utensils) sits close to or touches the underside of the hob, and whether there's any visible gap at the back of the unit. If it's tight or touching, that's probably your cause.
2. Do a test cook on high with the drawer left open a few inches. If it no longer cuts out, or lasts much longer, that suggests it's airflow, not a faulty part.
3. Next time the code flashes, take a short phone video of the display. You can then play it back slowly and read it. A temperature or overheat-type code would back this up. Something else would point more towards a sensor or board. If the open-drawer test fixes it, the real cure is restoring the clearance. Emptying the top drawer and keeping it shallow may help, but often the fitter needs to lower the drawer runners, fit a spacer or ventilation panel, or open up the back. Samsung's installation instructions for your hob list the required gap and ventilation, so it's worth showing those to whoever fitted the unit. Running the hob repeatedly into overheat cut-outs isn't great for the electronics long term, so it's worth sorting. If it still cuts out even with the drawer open and plenty of air, then a temperature sensor, the fan or the power board become the suspects. That would need an engineer, since the hob has to come out.
ok i can open the drawer and look with a torch i guess. but wont be pulling anything out or lifting the hob. does it cool down and work again after a few mins? yeah it does

First switch it off at the wall or cooker switch and let it cool completely. Yes, and that's what makes this fairly clear. A hob that cuts out, then works again after a few minutes of cooling, is behaving exactly as its overheat protection is designed to. Add the fan running flat out first and the timing (it started when the drawer unit went in), and restricted airflow underneath is by far the most likely cause. A failing sensor or power board can mimic this, but they don't usually line up so neatly with a change to the cabinet. You don't need to lift or remove anything. These are enough: 1. Torch look, with the hob off and cool and the drawer just opened. If the drawer box, or pans and lids stacked in it, sit within a finger's width of the hob's underside, or the back of the unit is fully boarded with no gap, that's your answer.
2. Take anything tall out of the top drawer so nothing sits near the hob base. Then cook on high again. If it lasts noticeably longer, that suggests it's airflow.
3. In the meantime, ease the load. Use a medium-high setting rather than boost, and avoid running several zones on high at once. Less heat means fewer cut-outs while you get it sorted. If the torch check shows it's tight, the proper fix is for whoever fitted the drawer unit to restore the clearance Samsung specifies in the hob's installation instructions. That usually means lowering the top drawer runners, fitting a shallower drawer, or opening a vent gap at the back. It's their installation, so it's reasonable to ask them to put it right. If there's clearly plenty of space and it still cuts out just as fast, then a sensor, fan or board fault moves up the list. That would be an engineer job. Let me know what you see with the torch.
ok ill have a look with the torch. not moving anything else tho. if its tight what then, just get the fitter back?

Yes. If the torch shows it's tight, getting the fitter back is the right move, and you shouldn't need to touch anything yourself. The fault is in how the unit sits under the hob, not in the hob, so it's theirs to put right. To make that conversation easy:
1. Take a quick photo with the torch showing the gap, or lack of one, between the drawer and the hob's underside, and the back of the unit.
2. Note the pattern: it started when the unit went in, the fan roars, and it cuts out after 5–10 minutes on high then works again once cooled. That points clearly at overheating from poor airflow.
3. Ask them to check the clearance and ventilation in Samsung's installation instructions for the hob. If you don't have the paperwork, it's usually downloadable from Samsung's website using the model number on the hob's label or manual. Typical fixes are lowering the top drawer runners, fitting a shallower drawer or a spacer panel, or opening a vent gap at the back. If the gap looks generous and there's a clear route for air at the back, the fitter isn't the answer. A sensor, fan or board fault becomes more likely, and that's a job for a Samsung or appliance engineer. Either way, until it's sorted, medium-high rather than boost will cut down the overheating. Let me know what the torch shows and I'll tell you which way it points.
